newsitem.title: USA: Texas girds for record-setting week of execution.
newsitem.headline: Texas girds for record-setting week of execution.

text.p: Five executions are set to be carried out in Texas over the next week, heightening tensions on the state's death row and renewing concerns about new laws limiting the appeals of death row inmates nationwide.

A year after state and federal courts upheld laws designed to cut the average nine-year stay on death row nearly in half, a record number of executions are expected both in Texas and the United States this year, officials said.

But death penalty opponents called this a rush to judgment and said that the pace, combined with the shear number of people on death row nationwide the odds of an innocent person being put to death had increased.

"We are really getting into a precarious situation regarding executing an innocent person," Lisa Bartle of the Death Penalty Information Centre said. "Texas has been moving at a much faster pace than other states, but even in Texas the rate that they are going at now is unprecedented."

Beginning with Friday's execution of a convicted murderer, five executions are docketed through next Thursday in Texas. Another five are set for June, putting the state on a pace to execute 20 people by mid-year and eclipse its record of 19 in a single year.

Of the 22 executions in the United States so far this year, 10 have been in Texas. The state leads the nation with 117 executions since capital punishment was reinstated by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1976.

Last year, though, the Huntsville prison death chamber fell nearly silent. As a challenge to a state law streamlining the death penalty appeals worked its way through the courts, three men sealed their fate by waiving appeals but more than two dozen won temporary reprieves, prosecutors said.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals last fall upheld the state law, and a sense of urgency heightened on the state's death row in recent months as delayed executions were rescheduled, a prison spokesman said.

"They were sort of hinging their hopes on that decision, and with that gone they don't have anything left," Nunnelee said. "The majority of these guys have been there for 10 years or more, so their time is up."

Death penalty opponents acknowledge that a majority of Americans support the death penalty in murder cases. That support is mirrored in a push to limit appeals and expand capital punishment as a sentence in drunken driving and other cases where victims are killed, they said.

"More and more states are expanding what crimes the prosecution can seek the death penalty in," Bartle said. Federal anti-terrorism legislation passed in the aftermath of the Oklahoma City bombing also limited the scope of federal appeals in state capital punishment cases, she said.

Texas prison officials expect this week's unprecedented number of executions to be carried out without a hitch in the nation's busiest death chamber -- a blue-tiled room equipped with a hospital gurney and a glass partition separating the condemned from members of his and his victims' families.
"There's no special preparations. We've done two in one night before," Texas Department of Corrections spokesman Larry Todd said. "There's an emotional toll, but we can cope."
